name: Experts React
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Kallisto Medium with picked words in Kallisto Heavy, on a navy
card, in three colours offered for the type and the same three for
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.

_comment_face: Kallisto Medium. Which cut that is, why the full name rather than
'Kallisto' is declared, and what the machine may already know it
by are written out in content/faces/kallisto-medium.json rather
than repeated here.
It is a wide squarish techno sans, and the width is the one thing
about it worth knowing before a caption is set on it. Its capitals
average 0.753em, which makes it the widest block face under this
heading, and at the preset's 40px on a 540-wide frame that is
about 27px a character against the 486px a line has. So the lines
break at roughly eighteen characters and the preset's `maxChars`
of 20 is never what stops them: of the two ceilings the preset
states, the width is the one this face runs into first.
That is a fact to know rather than a problem to fix. The two
ceilings exist to ask different questions - what the frame holds,
and what a viewer reads at a glance (see `maxChars` in
js/channels.js) - and a face wide enough to answer the first more
strictly than the second is a face whose lines are already inside
what a glance reads. Hall of Femme is the other way round at
0.660em, where twenty characters fit the width and the character
ceiling is what breaks the line.
A 500-weight face is legible over a photograph for the reason Hall
of Femme's 200-weight one is: it is not over the photograph at
all, it is on a card in a colour somebody chose. On this show the
argument is barely needed - the Medium is a solid mid weight with
squared, closed forms and would hold its own on a still - but the
card is what makes the weight a choice instead of a risk taken
forty times a run.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the three in `colors`
below, so the yellow swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is
found by matching this value rather than by being listed first.
Acid yellow on the navy card is the pairing this show opens on,
and unlike the orange-carded pack under this heading there is
nothing to weigh: #E7FE01 on #0C0938 is 16.7 to 1, well past any
threshold anybody would hold a caption to. Both of the show's own
colours are in that pairing - the yellow is what reads as the
brand and the navy is the ground it reads against - so the default
is the show rather than a compromise between it and legibility.
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - three buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same three in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does and for their reason: the point
is the PAIRING. Nine combinations of the acid yellow, an absolute
white and the navy, and the ones worth having are the ones that
read. A palette that could only ever be used one way round would
be a palette of three cards, and this show's look is the pairing
rather than any one of them.
Which ones read is unusually lopsided here, and it is worth having
written down rather than discovered: the navy is the only dark
colour of the three, so it is one half of every pairing that
works. Yellow on navy is 16.7 to 1, white on navy 18.9, and both
of those the other way up. The two light colours against each
other are 1.1 to 1 - a yellow caption on a white card is not a
weak pairing, it is an invisible one.
That is not an oversight either, and it is Hall of Femme's
argument applied to a palette that happens to be two lights and a
dark. The two lists are independent because the pairing is the
feature, and a rule barring the combinations that do not read
would cost the panel more explaining than an invisible caption
costs a user, who can see it is invisible and presses another
swatch.
The absolute white is meant as written: #FFFFFF, not an off-white
pulled towards either of the others. It is the show's second way
of setting type on the navy and the only alternative to the
yellow, so what it is for is being the neutral - a white with a
cast in it would be a third brand colour nobody chose.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the brand
yellow, the neutral, the ground - and the two defaults are picked
out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens on the
first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom Hall of
Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one order.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Kallisto Heavy, in the same colour as the
rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and rap-lore's both.
500 against 900 is nearly the whole of what this family has, and
it is a loud highlight - closer to Hall of Femme's 200 against 800
than to rap-lore's single step of Montserrat. It can be, because
these two cuts are within two percent of each other in width
(0.753em against 0.768em): the picked word arrives heavier without
arriving wider, so the sentence keeps the rhythm it was wrapped
with and the card keeps its shape. Hall of Femme's two cuts are
ten percent apart on that measure and the highlight works there
too - this is the same gesture with less of that cost, not a
quieter one.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Navy, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching
this value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be
written in the order the show states its colours in while the
channel still opens on yellow type and a navy card.
#0C0938 is the darkest card under this heading, where the
neighbours run to pinks, magentas, reds and one orange, and that
is what makes this show itself at a glance: the card is the shape
that is a fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it, so
it is what carries the colour, and the type is what has to stay
legible against it. A near-black navy is also the one ground both
of the show's other colours read on, which is why the note on
`colors` above can be so short about which pairings work.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
